eyebrow: KEY STAGE 3 HISTORY • YEAR 7 THEMATIC CHRONOLOGY • 18 MILESTONES

eras.title: Part 1: Roman Water Engineering, Baths & Imperial Collapse (AD 43–410)
Part 2: Medieval Boroughs, Monasteries & The Black Death (1100–1388)
Part 3: Early Modern London, Private Water & The Great Plague (1500–1665)
Part 4: Industrial Slums, Cholera, Sewers & The Sanitary Revolution (1780–1900)

milestones.title: Roman Conquest of Britain & Gravity-Fed Stone Aqueducts
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Did Roman water engineering protect ordinary Britons or showcase imperial luxury?
milestones.imageCaption: Roman gravity-fed stone aqueduct (1st century AD): Engineered on a gentle downward slope to carry millions of gallons of pure upland spring water into towns.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Roman Britain (AD 43–410)—towns, aqueducts, baths, and stone sewers from Londinium and Aquae Sulis to Hadrian’s Wall.
milestones.catalyst: Emperor Claudius’s **AD 43 conquest** packed thousands of soldiers and townsfolk into walled cities like **Londinium** and **Eboracum**, overwhelming Iron Age shallow field cesspits.
milestones.turningPoint: Roman military engineers surveyed upland springs and built gently sloped stone **aqueducts** feeding **castella** water towers, street fountains, and elite villas.
milestones.impact: Fresh running water supplied booming provincial capitals while projecting **Romanitas**—the pride and technological power of imperial Rome.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Piped aqueduct water made possible the centerpiece of Roman urban daily life: heated communal bathhouses and stone latrines.

keyTerms.definition: A monumental bridge or masonry channel engineered to convey fresh spring water over long distances using gravity.
The cultural, political, and technological ideals of Roman imperial civilization and power.

milestones.title: Public Thermae, Hypocaust Heating & Hidden Parasite Hazards
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Did Roman water engineering protect ordinary Britons or showcase imperial luxury?
milestones.imageCaption: Excavated Roman hypocaust pilae brick stacks at Aquae Sulis (Bath): Hot furnace air circulated beneath mosaic bathhouse floors.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Major bathhouses and military latrines across Roman Britannia, including Aquae Sulis and Housesteads Fort.
milestones.catalyst: For a tiny copper coin, Roman townsfolk visited public **thermae** heated by underground **hypocaust** furnaces, scraping away sweat and oil with curved bronze **strigils**.
milestones.turningPoint: Wastewater from bathhouses continuously flushed stone multi-seater **latrines**, yet bathers shared a communal sponge stick (**tersorium**) and drank from toxic **lead pipes**.
milestones.impact: Because Romans lacked germ knowledge and rarely drained warm pools, townspeople still suffered **whipworm**, dysentery, and chronic lead poisoning (**plumbism**).
milestones.bridgeToNext: Even this impressive stonework depended completely on Roman taxes and legions—which vanished abruptly in AD 410.

keyTerms.definition: Large, state-run public bathhouses equipped with heated pools, exercise yards, and social meeting spaces.
An underground Roman central heating system where furnace heat and hot smoke circulated beneath suspended floors.
A natural sea sponge affixed to a wooden stick, used communally to clean oneself in Roman latrines.

milestones.title: Roman Withdrawal & The Thousand-Year Urban Sanitation Gap
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Did Roman water engineering protect ordinary Britons or showcase imperial luxury?
milestones.imageCaption: Inscribed Roman lead water pipe (fistula) from Aquae Sulis (Roman Baths Museum): Abandoned or melted down after Roman administration ended in AD 410.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Provincial Roman water networks left without imperial upkeep after the legions withdrew in AD 410.
milestones.catalyst: Roman aqueducts, baths, and sewers relied entirely on centralized imperial taxation, military engineers, and municipal maintenance crews.
milestones.turningPoint: When **Roman legions withdrew from Britain in AD 410**, urban administration collapsed overnight; stone aqueducts silted up and lead pipes were stripped for scrap.
milestones.impact: Britain entered a **thousand-year gap** without municipal piped water, leaving growing medieval towns to rely once more on rivers and shallow wells.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Only wealthy medieval monasteries preserved clean piped water systems while crowded market boroughs grew outside their walls.

keyTerms.definition: Chronic, toxic lead poisoning caused by consuming water or wine conveyed through lead pipes and lead-lined cookware.
A communal multi-seater public toilet consisting of stone benches set over a deep running-water sewer ditch.

milestones.title: Canterbury Priory’s Five Settling Tanks & Monastic Clean Water
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did medieval towns struggle so badly to keep streets and water clean?
milestones.imageCaption: Eadwine Psalter Waterworks Plan of Christ Church Priory, Canterbury (c. 1165, Trinity College Cambridge): Channelling hilltop spring water through five settling tanks.
milestones.catalyst: Protected inside quiet walled cloisters and funded by rich land endowments, medieval monks prized ritual cleanliness and pure drinking water.
milestones.turningPoint: Around **1165**, Prior Wibert engineered **Canterbury Priory’s** lead-pipe system, passing hilltop spring water through **five settling tanks** into kitchens, **lavatorium** basins, and flushed latrines.
milestones.impact: Monasteries like **Canterbury** and **Titchfield Abbey** enjoyed far healthier lives than ordinary townsfolk, proving clean water existed where wealth and space allowed.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Outside monastery walls, booming medieval market boroughs faced overflowing cesspits, butcher waste, and muddy lanes.

keyTerms.definition: A stone reservoir designed to slow water flow so that suspended sand, silt, and mud sink to the bottom, purifying the water.
A dedicated stone washing trough or circular fountain located outside a monastic dining refectory for communal handwashing.

milestones.title: Medieval Market Boroughs, Cesspits, Rakers & Gong Farmers
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did medieval towns struggle so badly to keep streets and water clean?
milestones.imageCaption: Overhanging timber-framed jetties on The Shambles, York: Narrow medieval butcher lanes where offal and workshop waste ran down open street gutters.
milestones.catalyst: Rapidly growing **medieval boroughs** like London, York, and Coventry lacked underground sewers while butchers, tanners, and dyers dumped blood, urine, and dyes into streets and rivers.
milestones.turningPoint: Town councils hired street **rakers**, fined polluters in **Court Leet** hearings, and households paid nocturnal **gong farmers** to shovel out backyard **cesspits**.
milestones.impact: Despite genuine civic efforts, unlined cesspits still leaked into shallow garden wells and polluted rivers used downstream for drinking water.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In the summer of 1348, an invisible killer carried by rat fleas overwhelmed every medieval town defence.

keyTerms.definition: A self-governing medieval town granted a royal charter with the right to hold regular markets and run local courts.
A nocturnal specialist labourer hired to dig out and remove raw human sewage from domestic cesspits.
A deep pit lined with dry stone or timber, dug beneath or behind houses to collect household toilet waste.

milestones.title: The Black Death Catastrophe & Miasma Theory
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did medieval towns struggle so badly to keep streets and water clean?
milestones.imageCaption: Josse Lieferinxe, Saint Sebastian Interceding for the Plague-Stricken (1497–1499, Walters Art Museum): Mass plague burials outside medieval city walls.
milestones.catalyst: In summer **1348**, the **Black Death** (*Yersinia pestis* spread by fleas on black rats) entered English ports and killed **30% to 50%** of Britain’s people in eighteen months.
milestones.turningPoint: Ignorant of bacteria, doctors blamed planetary alignments, God’s wrath, and foul-smelling **miasma** air, while councils imposed **40-day ship quarantines** and dug mass burial trenches.
milestones.impact: Although miasma theory missed rat fleas completely, fear of bad smells spurred towns and Parliament to pass tougher laws against street filth.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Convinced foul river smells bred plague, Parliament passed England’s first national clean-water law in 1388.

keyTerms.definition: The catastrophic pandemic of bubonic and pneumonic plague that struck Britain in 1348, killing up to half the population.
The incorrect medical belief that infectious diseases were generated and transmitted by toxic, foul-smelling air.

milestones.title: Parliament Passes the 1388 Statute of Cambridge
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did medieval towns struggle so badly to keep streets and water clean?
milestones.imageCaption: Medieval parchment court roll recording municipal fines against householders and traders who polluted lanes and ditches.
milestones.catalyst: Repeated waves of fourteenth-century plague convinced royal officials and borough leaders like Coventry’s council that rotting offal and river dung endangered public health.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1388**, King Richard II’s Parliament passed the **Statute of Cambridge**, threatening heavy **£20 fines** for dumping animal guts, dung, or rubbish into rivers and ditches.
milestones.impact: As historian **Carole Rawcliffe** proved, medieval people cared about clean water, but tiny town budgets lacked pumps, pipes, and enforcement power.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Between 1500 and 1665, London’s population exploded past 500,000—pushing old Tudor wells and cesspits past breaking point.

keyTerms.definition: A 1388 parliamentary law passed under Richard II banning the disposal of animal dung, offal, and refuse into public rivers and ditches.
A self-governing medieval town granted a royal charter with the right to hold regular markets and run local courts.

milestones.title: Sir John Harington Invents the ‘Ajax’ Flush Water Closet
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did rapid growth make Tudor and Stuart London filthier and deadlier?
milestones.imageCaption: Sir John Harington (Wellcome Collection): Queen Elizabeth I’s godson who fitted England’s first valve-flushing water closet at Richmond Palace in 1596.
milestones.catalyst: As Tudor **London** boomed toward a crowded **metropolis**, even royal palaces suffered foul smells from indoor chamber pots and wooden close-stools.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1596**, Queen Elizabeth I’s godson **Sir John Harington** invented the **‘Ajax’ flushing water closet** at **Richmond Palace**, using an overhead cistern and brass valve.
milestones.impact: Without pressurized street water mains or underground sewers, Harington’s toilet stayed a rare royal novelty while ordinary families kept using cesspits.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Poisoned parish wells soon inspired wealthy London entrepreneurs to pipe clean spring water in for paying customers.

keyTerms.definition: An early flush toilet system that washed human excrement away through a drain pipe using water from a cistern.
A very large, densely populated commercial and cultural capital city, such as seventeenth-century London.

milestones.title: Sir Hugh Myddelton Opens the 38-Mile New River to London
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did rapid growth make Tudor and Stuart London filthier and deadlier?
milestones.imageCaption: Wenceslaus Hollar, Etching of the New River Head and Water House at Islington (1665): Terminal reservoir of Sir Hugh Myddelton’s 38-mile freshwater canal.
milestones.catalyst: Leaking backyard cesspits poisoned Stuart London’s parish wells, creating huge commercial demand among wealthy households for clean drinking water.
milestones.turningPoint: Financed by goldsmith **Sir Hugh Myddelton**, workers dug the **38-mile New River** (opened **1613**) from **Hertfordshire** springs to **Islington**, piping water through hollowed **elm tree trunks**.
milestones.impact: Clean piped water reached rich merchants who paid yearly fees, leaving poorer slum families drinking dirty Thames water or buying buckets from carriers.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Even wealthy Londoners could not escape underground filth when neighbours’ brick cesspits cracked beneath crowded streets.

keyTerms.definition: A 38-mile man-made fresh water aqueduct canal opened in 1613 to bring drinking water from Hertfordshire to London.
A very large, densely populated commercial and cultural capital city, such as seventeenth-century London.

milestones.title: Overcrowded Stuart London & Samuel Pepys’s Sewage-Flooded Cellar
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did rapid growth make Tudor and Stuart London filthier and deadlier?
milestones.imageCaption: John Hayls, Portrait of Samuel Pepys (1666, National Portrait Gallery): Restoration diarist who recorded stepping into neighbour sewage in his cellar in October 1660.
milestones.catalyst: By **1660**, London crammed nearly **500,000 people** into overhanging timber tenements built above poorly mortared brick cellars and overflowing **nightsoil** vaults.
milestones.turningPoint: On **20 October 1660**, Admiralty official **Samuel Pepys** walked into his Seething Lane basement and stepped straight into raw waste leaking through his neighbour’s cracked cesspit wall.
milestones.impact: Pepys’s diary proved that without city drains, even wealthy officials lived inches from seeping sewage and depended on midnight filth carts.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Five years later, crammed wooden alleys and rat-infested rubbish heaps fuelled Stuart London’s worst epidemic.

keyTerms.definition: Human feces collected at night from household cesspits and privies, used as agricultural manure.
A deep pit lined with dry stone or timber, dug beneath or behind houses to collect household toilet waste.

milestones.title: The Great Plague of 1665 & Weekly Bills of Mortality
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did rapid growth make Tudor and Stuart London filthier and deadlier?
milestones.imageCaption: London Bill of Mortality for 12–19 September 1665 (Wellcome Collection), recording a devastating weekly peak of 7,165 plague burials.
milestones.catalyst: In **1665**, bubonic plague swept Stuart London’s rat-infested alleys, killing over **100,000 people** while parish **Searchers of the Dead** tallied deaths in **Bills of Mortality**.
milestones.turningPoint: Still blaming **miasma**, officials locked stricken families behind red-crossed doors, burned street fires, and slaughtered **40,000 dogs and 200,000 cats** that hunted rats.
milestones.impact: Epidemic medicine remained trapped in miasma dogma even as the **1666 Great Fire** burned away London’s worst medieval timber slums.
milestones.bridgeToNext: After 1780, steam-powered factory boomtowns created even deadlier industrial slums—and welcomed a new waterborne killer.

keyTerms.definition: Weekly published statistical mortality sheets in London recording numbers of burials and causes of death by parish.
Elderly women appointed by parish authorities during plague outbreaks to inspect corpses and confirm causes of death.

milestones.title: Industrial Back-to-Back Slums & The 1831 Asiatic Cholera Shock
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did cholera and the 1858 ‘Great Stink’ force London to build sewers?
milestones.imageCaption: John Leech, ‘A Court for King Cholera’ (Punch, 1852): Exposing overcrowded Victorian slum courts, overflowing dungheaps, and contaminated water.
milestones.catalyst: **Industrialisation** crammed factory workers in Manchester, Leeds, and London into airless **back-to-back slums** where **60 people** shared one overflowing **privy** and life spans fell to **19 years**.
milestones.turningPoint: In **October 1831**, waterborne **Asiatic cholera** (‘the Blue Death’) arrived in **Sunderland** and killed over **52,000 Britons** while doctors uselessly burned tar barrels against miasma.
milestones.impact: Cholera’s terrifying speed shocked Victorian Britain and forced reformers to investigate the filth of industrial slums.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Civil servant Edwin Chadwick compiled nationwide death statistics to prove slum dirt was bankrupting taxpayers.

keyTerms.definition: The rapid shift from agricultural craftwork to steam-powered factory mass production in cities.
A lethal, waterborne bacterial disease causing rapid dehydration, diarrhea, and death within hours.
An outdoor latrine shed situated above an open cesspool or collection bucket.

milestones.title: Edwin Chadwick’s 1842 Sanitary Report & Permissive 1848 Act
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did cholera and the 1858 ‘Great Stink’ force London to build sewers?
milestones.imageCaption: Title page of Edwin Chadwick’s pioneering 1842 Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain.
milestones.catalyst: Most Victorian MPs followed **laissez-faire** beliefs, arguing government should leave local taxes low rather than interfere in housing or drains.
milestones.turningPoint: **Edwin Chadwick’s 1842 Sanitary Report** proved statistically that filthy slums caused disease and poverty, prompting Parliament to pass the **1848 Public Health Act**.
milestones.impact: Because the 1848 Act was **permissive** rather than compulsory, stingy **ratepayers** blocked expensive new sewers and cholera kept returning.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When cholera struck Soho again in August 1854, local physician Dr John Snow put miasma theory to the test.

keyTerms.definition: The political belief that government should not interfere in the economy, businesses, or public life.
A local property owner who pays local taxes (rates) to fund municipal government services.

milestones.title: Dr John Snow’s Soho Spot Map & Removal of the Broad Street Handle
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did science and government laws finally defeat water-borne cholera?
milestones.imageCaption: Dr John Snow’s 1854 Soho cholera spot map (Wellcome Collection), plotting 616 local cholera deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Dr John Snow’s 1854 Soho Broad Street investigation alongside Sir Joseph Bazalgette’s London intercepting sewers.
milestones.catalyst: In late August **1854**, a fierce cholera outbreak killed **616 people** around **Broad Street, Soho**, while health boards still blamed poisonous cesspool air.
milestones.turningPoint: **Dr John Snow** mapped every death on a **spot map**, noted beer-drinking **Lion Brewery** workers stayed healthy, and persuaded officials on **8 September** to remove the **Broad Street pump handle**.
milestones.impact: Reverend **Henry Whitehead** traced the leak to a cracked cesspool at **40 Broad Street** three feet away, proving cholera spread through **dirty water**, though miasma believers still doubted Snow.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Four summers later, a baking heatwave turned the sewage-choked River Thames into an unbearable crisis right outside Parliament.

keyTerms.definition: The branch of medical science studying the spread, causes, and control of diseases in populations.
A cartographic map that plots the exact locations of disease cases to identify a common outbreak source.

milestones.title: The Great Stink of the Thames Shatters Parliamentary Delay
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did cholera and the 1858 ‘Great Stink’ force London to build sewers?
milestones.imageCaption: John Leech, ‘Father Thames Introducing His Offspring to the Fair City of London’ (Punch, July 1858), published during the Great Stink.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The tidal River Thames at Westminster during the June 1858 Great Stink.
milestones.catalyst: By 1855, **200,000 flushing water closets** emptied raw waste straight into the River Thames, which scientist **Michael Faraday** warned had become an opaque sewer.
milestones.turningPoint: In **June 1858**, **35°C summer heat** baked the Thames mud into **The Great Stink**; lime-soaked curtains failed to protect Westminster, and panicked MPs voted **£3 million** in eighteen days.
milestones.impact: Direct misery in Parliament finally broke **laissez-faire** delay and funded Chief Engineer **Joseph Bazalgette** to rebuild London’s entire drainage network.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While Bazalgette’s navvies tunnelled beneath London, French chemist Louis Pasteur uncovered the true microscopic cause of disease.

keyTerms.definition: An underground brick pit or holding tank for untreated domestic sewage and human waste.
The political belief that government should not interfere in the economy, businesses, or public life.

milestones.title: Louis Pasteur’s Swan-Neck Flasks & The Germ Theory of Disease
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did science and government laws finally defeat water-borne cholera?
milestones.imageCaption: Louis Pasteur’s 1861 swan-neck flask experiment disproving spontaneous generation and proving microscopic germs cause decay and disease.
milestones.catalyst: Even after Snow’s 1854 map, stubborn doctors clung to **miasma** and **spontaneous generation** because nobody had proven invisible microbes caused illness.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1861**, French chemist **Louis Pasteur** used boiled broth inside curved **swan-neck flasks** to publish **Germ Theory**, proving living microscopic organisms soured liquids and spread disease.
milestones.impact: Pasteur’s breakthrough overturned centuries of miasma guesswork and gave public health campaigners solid laboratory science.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Four years later, Joseph Bazalgette switched on the giant steam pumps of London’s new subterranean brick sewer network.

keyTerms.definition: The scientific principle proven by Louis Pasteur that diseases are caused by microscopic living organisms.
The disproven theory that living organisms could suddenly arise from non-living matter or rotting filth.

milestones.title: Sir Joseph Bazalgette’s 82 Miles of Intercepting Sewers Open
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was there rapid progress in Public Health between 1800 and 1900?
milestones.imageCaption: Sir Joseph Bazalgette’s Abbey Mills Pumping Station (1865–1868), nicknamed the ‘Cathedral of Sewage’, lifting London’s waste toward the tidal Thames.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Bazalgette’s 82 miles of Northern and Southern Intercepting Sewers and steam pumping stations at Abbey Mills and Crossness.
milestones.catalyst: Armed with Parliament’s £3 million grant after the Great Stink, Chief Engineer **Sir Joseph Bazalgette** designed a monumental gravity drainage system for London.
milestones.turningPoint: Using **318 million bricks** and waterproof **Portland cement**, navvies built **82 miles of intercepting sewers** and giant steam pumping stations at **Crossness (opened April 1865)** and **Abbey Mills**.
milestones.impact: Carrying **420 million gallons** of waste eastward daily away from drinking intakes, Bazalgette’s sewers permanently ended cholera in connected areas of London.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Clean sewers saved London, yet only a compulsory national law could force every town council across Britain to follow suit.

keyTerms.definition: Large subterranean brick tunnels designed to catch sewage before it enters a river and carry it away.
The design and construction of public infrastructure like bridges, tunnels, canals, and sewer systems.

milestones.title: Compulsory 1875 Public Health Act & Koch’s Cholera Bacterium
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was there rapid progress in Public Health between 1800 and 1900?
milestones.imageCaption: Eastney Beam Engine House, Portsmouth (1887): Municipal steam sewage pumping station built as British councils enforced the compulsory 1875 Public Health Act.
milestones.catalyst: After **working-class town men won the vote in 1867**, politicians could no longer ignore slum deaths or let local ratepayers dodge clean-water taxes.
milestones.turningPoint: Prime Minister **Benjamin Disraeli** passed the **compulsory 1875 Public Health Act** mandating clean water, covered sewers, and **Medical Officers of Health**, before **Robert Koch** isolated the cholera **bacterium** in **1884**.
milestones.impact: Combining epidemiology, civil engineering, germ science, and compulsory state law conquered waterborne cholera and raised British urban life expectancy by 1900.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Lasting Legacy: Clean piped water and municipal sewerage shifted from imperial Roman luxury into a universal legal right across modern Britain.

keyTerms.definition: Required by law; mandatory, leaving no choice or option to local authorities.
A legally mandated municipal doctor appointed by local councils to inspect and safeguard public health.
A microscopic single-celled organism, some of which cause infectious diseases like cholera.
